Privacy Effective October 27, 2026. Material changes will be posted here with a new effective date; account holders get an email when a change affects them. CommuteScout is an independent, one-person project. The short version: the map and assistant work without an account and store nothing that identifies you; if you create an account, we store your email and what you save to it (watch areas, places, reports, plugin choices, API keys), because that is what those features are; nothing is sold, there are no ads, and there is no cross-site tracking. What we collect Without an account (the map, route planner, and assistant): questions you ask the assistant are logged to improve answers, tied to a salted daily hash instead of your address, with coordinates rounded to about a kilometer. If you press the "Was this right?" thumbs, that vote is logged with the question the same way and reviewed to improve answers. Route and address searches are processed to answer them and appear in the same anonymized logs. The map opens on your approximate area so you do not have to scroll to it: our CDN derives a city-level position from your IP address, rounded to about a kilometer, and we use it only to choose that first view. It is never stored or logged, and no location permission is requested. If that lookup is unavailable, your browser's timezone (read locally, never sent to us) picks a region instead. To show conditions, the map sends us the area or route on screen; our request logs drop precise positions, except for requests that failed with a server error, which we keep to fix the failure. No cookies are set. Your browser keeps a few settings in local storage: the base map you picked, the plugins you switched on or off, and the email you typed to sign in. They stay on your device, except that the plugin switches travel with a report you post, so it reaches only the plugins you use. If you share a trip : the trip you share (the start and end names, the route, and its directions) is stored so the link works, and anyone with the link can open it. It is not tied to an account and is deleted after 180 days. With an account : your email address, your sign-in identity from Google, Apple, or the email link you used, and what you save: Watch areas you draw (names, shapes, alert settings) and, if you enable notifications, the push subscription for each device. Alert emails are delivered through Resend. Places you save or go to (Home, Work, favorites, and recent destinations), so they follow you between devices. Your plugin choices: the plugins you switched off, and any private plugin you added by address, with the access token you gave it. Reports you post on the map (what you saw, where, which way you were heading, and any note), linked to your account so daily limits and votes work. Others see the report on the map without your identity until it expires, between 20 minutes and a day depending on the kind. It is also sent to the public plugins you have switched on that accept reports, under a separate pseudonym for each plugin, never your account or email. API keys: the name you give each key, a one-way hash of its secret, and when it was created and last used. Each keyed request is logged with the key id, the tool, and the result, to count it against the daily allowance. The CommuteScout Drive apps (iPhone and Android): your device's location is used on the phone to guide you and to ask us for alerts along your route, which reach us the same way map requests do. Downloaded maps and voices, and the drive log, stay on the phone; the drive log leaves it only if you share it from Settings. The apps contain no analytics or advertising code. Some plugins answer the app directly: when you switch one on, it sees the area you are driving through, and a plugin that shows alerts meant for you also receives a sign-in token that proves which account is asking. If you write to us (the contact form): the name, email address, and message you type. We use them to read and answer you, and for nothing else. The message is delivered to us as email; we do not add you to any list. If you join the Pro waitlist : your email address, and nothing else. We use it once, to tell you when Pro launches. Ask us at any time to remove it. Analytics : cookieless Cloudflare Web Analytics counts visits and page timings. It sets no cookies, stores no device identifiers, and does not follow you to other sites. Who touches the data Categories of third parties that process data to run the service. None of them get your data for their own marketing, and we do not sell or rent anything: Google Cloud and Firebase host the service, sign-ins, and the database that stores accounts and watch areas. Anthropic processes assistant questions to generate answers. Resend delivers alert and sign-in emails, and the messages you send through the contact form. Cloudflare provides the cookieless visit counts and serves the downloadable map files. Apple and Google distribute the apps and deliver their push notifications. Plugin operators receive reports and votes under a pseudonym, as described above, and the requests of apps that use their plugin directly. TomTom provides live traffic speeds; the server sends it road coordinates being checked, never your identity. State transportation agencies publish the public road data shown for their states (WSDOT, Oregon DOT TripCheck, OHGO, UDOT, ADOT, Alaska DOT&PF, CDOT, FDOT, VDOT SmarterRoads, Idaho 511, 511NY, WisDOT, INDOT, MnDOT, KDOT, NJDOT, MDOT SHA, MDOT MiDrive, MDOT Traffic Mississippi, MoDOT, TravelMidwest/IDOT, ALGO Traffic/ALDOT, NCDOT, Iowa DOT, KYTC, Oklahoma DOT, HDOT, Louisiana DOTD, DelDOT, TDOT SmartWay, the City of Austin, and the NE Compass portal for Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont). Our server fetches their public feeds; they never receive anything about you. Camera snapshots load in your browser directly from the agency's image host, which sees the request the way any image load does. Stadia Maps provides routing and address lookup; it sees the coordinates and place names involved in what you look up, as our server queries it. OpenFreeMap serves the tiles for the Positron and Bright base maps; when you use one of them, your browser requests tiles from tiles.openfreemap.org, which sees your IP address and the map area you are viewing. The other base maps are drawn from files we host. Map data comes from OpenStreetMap contributors. Review, change, delete Signed-in users can see every watch area on the watch page , edit or delete any of them, and delete the whole account with the "Delete my account" button there - that immediately removes the account record (with your saved places and plugin choices), all watch areas, alert state, push subscriptions, and API keys. Reports you posted expire on their own within two days. Anything else, or any question about data we hold: email privacy@commutescout.com . Do Not Track We do not respond to Do Not Track signals, because there is nothing to turn off: no advertising trackers, no cross-site tracking, and no cookies on the public site. No other parties conduct cross-site tracking through this service. Where and how long Data lives in Google Cloud's us-west1 region. Anonymized question logs and request logs age out with normal log retention (about 30 days). Account data stays until you delete it. Reports are deleted from storage two days after they are posted, and shared trips after 180 days. Push subscriptions are dropped automatically when a device unsubscribes. Contact messages stay in our email until we have dealt with them. A waitlist email stays until Pro launches or until you ask us to remove it, whichever comes first. Separately, we keep a long-term archive of the public road events themselves (incidents, closures, fires, as the agencies publish them) to build history features; it contains no user data of any kind. Contact hello@commutescout.com (privacy requests: privacy@commutescout.com ). The code behind the service is open source at github.com/nicglazkov/commutescout , so you can check any of this yourself.
